questions.q: Who is the author of "dkys es?kk ikuh ns" and what is his primary literary region? (Recall level)
questions.a: The author is Shekhar Joshi (शेखर जोशी), born in 1926 in Bageshwar, Uttarakhand. His primary literary region is the Kumaon hills of Uttarakhand, and he is known for portraying the lives, struggles, and dialect of ordinary hill people. A wrong answer (e.g., naming Premchand or placing him in Rajasthan) reveals the student has not read the introductory note and cannot anchor the story's dialect, setting, and cultural references — leading to misinterpretation of terms like "es<d&eaMyh" or the significance of "naula" (spring).

questions.q: In your own words, explain why water scarcity in Uttarakhand hills is described as both a geographical and a social problem in the story's background. (Understand level)
questions.a: Geographically, the steep slopes cause rainwater to run off quickly, and natural springs (naulas) are the only source — but they are drying due to deforestation and reduced recharge. Socially, the powerful (vaèkfo'okl) capture these springs for hotels, agriculture, or private use, while the marginalized (es<d&eaMyh) are denied access. A wrong answer that says "only less rain" or "only rich people take it" misses the interplay: the geography makes water scarce, but the social structure decides who suffers. This misconception leads to treating the story as an environmental tale rather than a critique of power.

questions.q: Compare the narrator's perspective and "thth's" perspective on water distribution in the story. What does this contrast reveal about the story's central conflict? (Analyze level)
questions.a: The narrator (educated, outsider/observer) initially sees water scarcity as a natural hardship; "thth" (local, victim) exposes it as structural injustice — the powerful divert water for profit while the poor are criminalized for taking a pot. The contrast shifts the conflict from "man vs. nature" to "man vs. exploitative system." A wrong answer that calls it "two opinions" misses the epistemic hierarchy: the story validates the subaltern's analysis over the outsider's sympathy, a pattern in Joshi's work and Dalit/subaltern literature — crucial for theme questions in boards.

questions.q: The story ends with "thth" refusing to accept water as charity (cqokbZ) and demanding it as right. Evaluate whether this refusal is a practical solution or a symbolic act of resistance. Justify with textual reasoning. (Evaluate level)
questions.a: It is primarily symbolic resistance: practically, the family still needs water and the power structure remains; symbolically, "thth" rejects the frame of "beggar vs. giver" and asserts dignity — "ikuh dh cjcknh ugha, ikuh dk v?;Z" (not charity, but the value/price of water). A wrong answer calling it "foolish pride" imposes a middle-class pragmatism on a subaltern character, missing Joshi's intent: the story critiques a system where rights are packaged as charity. Board marking schemes reward answers that link character action to thematic statement.

questions.q: Write a 50-word "Before You Read" note for a Class 10 student explaining why they should care about a 1970s Uttarakhand water story today. Use at least two preview vocabulary words. (Create level)
questions.a: Sample: "This story isn't history — it's your future. When Bengaluru runs dry or Chennai trains water, it's the same injustice: the powerful (vaèkfo'okl) capture resources, the poor (es<d&eaMyh) queue for cqokbZ (charity). Joshi shows water isn't a gift but a right — and dignity means demanding it, not begging. Read to recognize the pattern." A poor answer summarizes plot ("a man wants water") showing the student cannot transfer context to present-day relevance — a core competency for CUET/board case-based questions.
